passages.text:
When Simon heard this, he said, “Will you not pressure me, after I have kept silent about his essence, to investigate only his purpose? For it is possible both to think and to speak about his essence—I mean by starting from the good qualities belonging to human beings. For example, being alive and being dead belong to a human being, but to God belongs not being dead, but being alive—and being alive eternally. Again, human beings can be evil or good, but to God belongs being incomparably good. And, so that I may not prolong the argument at length, the better of the qualities belonging to human beings belong eternally to God.”

Peter said, “Tell me, Simon: does it belong to human beings to beget evil and good people and to do evil and good things?”

Simon said, “It does.”

Peter said, “Since you have spoken this way, the better of the qualities belonging to human beings must be assigned to God. Since human beings beget evil and good people, God can beget only good people; and since human beings do evil and good things, he himself delights in doing only good things. Thus, concerning God, either it is possible not to speak of the qualities belonging to human beings and to remain silent, or it is reasonable to assign to him the better of the good qualities belonging to human beings. In this way, he alone is the cause of all good things.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Οὐ δυσωπήσεις με περὶ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτοῦ σιωπή[σαν]τα περὶ τῆς προαιρέσεως αὐτοῦ [ζη]τεῖν μόνης
lexical_decisions.chosen: Will you not pressure me, after I have kept silent about his essence, to investigate only his purpose?
lexical_decisions.rationale: δυσωπέω can mean to constrain, pressure, or shame someone into a course of action. The question form reflects οὐ, while “shame me ... into investigating” remains a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: about his essence
lexical_decisions.rationale: οὐσία denotes God’s being or essence here, whereas the plural οὐσίαι in the next section denotes elemental substances.

lexical_decisions.chosen: being alive and being dead
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect infinitive τεθνάναι denotes the state of having died or being dead, not merely the process of dying.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the better of the qualities belonging to human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσόντα denotes attributes or qualities that belong to someone, and κρείττονα selects those regarded as superior.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ δὲ θεῷ τὸ ἀσυγκρίτῳ ἀγαθῷ εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: to God belongs being incomparably good
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀσυγκρίτῳ may describe the good as incomparable or convey the adverbial sense “incomparably”; the latter produces natural English without changing the claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὕτως π[ερὶ θεοῦ] ἢ οὐ τὰ ἀνθρώποις προσόντα λέγειν καὶ σιωπᾶν ἔστιν ἢ τῶν ἀνθρώποις προσόντων κα[λῶν] εὖλογόν ἐστιν ἀπονέμειν αὐτῷ τὰ κ[ρείτ]τονα
lexical_decisions.chosen: Thus, concerning God, either it is possible not to speak of the qualities belonging to human beings and to remain silent, or it is reasonable to assign to him the better of the good qualities belonging to human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering lets ἔστιν govern the coordinated infinitives and takes οὐ directly with λέγειν: one may not speak and may remain silent. If οὐ is instead given wider scope, the first member could be read “it is not possible to speak of the qualities belonging to human beings and remain silent,” but that produces a less fitting contrast with the second alternative.

passages.text:
Simon said, “Therefore, if God is the cause only of good things, what remains to be thought except that some other first principle begot evil, or that it is perhaps unbegotten?”

Peter said, “Neither did some other power beget the evil one, nor is evil unbegotten, as I shall show at the end. For my present task is to demonstrate—as I promised at the beginning—that God is blameless in every respect. We have therefore granted that God possesses, beyond comparison, the better of the qualities belonging to human beings. Consequently, he may also be the one who puts forth the four substances—I mean hot and cold, wet and dry. These, being primary, simple, and unmixed, have an inclination toward neither side; but once put forth by God and blended outside him, they may become a living being possessing the purpose of destroying evil people. And so, since all things have been generated from him, the evil one neither comes from elsewhere nor has received his wickedness from God himself, who made everything and with whom it is impossible for wickedness to exist. For the substances, being neutral, were carefully distinguished and put forth from him; and when outside him they had been blended with one another by his skill, the desire for the destruction of evil people arose by an act of will. But the resulting evil cannot destroy good people, not even if it should wish to, for by law it has authority against those who sin. Thus, not knowing each person’s character, the evil one gains experience concerning them and, after thoroughly examining them, punishes them.”

Simon said, “Therefore, since God has the power to mix the elements and to make mixtures for whatever ends he wishes, so that whatever purposes he wishes may arise, why did he not make each person’s mixture disposed to choose good things?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ πονηρὸν ἑτέρα τις ἐγέννησεν ἀρχὴ ἢ ἄρ’ ἀγέννητόν ἐστιν;
lexical_decisions.chosen: some other first principle begot evil, or that it is perhaps unbegotten?
lexical_decisions.rationale: Simon uses the neuter τὸ πονηρόν and a neuter predicate, so “evil” and “it” preserve the wording. The personal interpretation “the evil one” is contextually possible, but Peter’s reply then observably shifts first to masculine τὸν πονηρόν and afterward back to neuter τὸ κακόν.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Οὔτε ἑτέρα τις δύναμις ἐγέννησεν τὸν πονηρὸν οὔτε ἀγέννητόν ἐστιν τὸ κακόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Neither did some other power beget the evil one, nor is evil unbegotten
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation preserves Peter’s transition from the masculine personal expression τὸν πονηρόν to the neuter abstraction τὸ κακόν.

lexical_decisions.chosen: some other first principle begot
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀρχή may denote a beginning, origin, source, or ruling first principle. “First principle” fits the proposed independent origin of evil, though “some other origin” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be the one who puts forth the four substances
lexical_decisions.rationale: προβολεύς describes one who projects or puts something forth. The rendering preserves the emanative image without importing a later technical system.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have an inclination toward neither side
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two opposed sides are left implicit in οὐδέτερον, contextually good and evil; the translation likewise leaves them unnamed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προβληθέντα δὲ ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ [κ]αὶ ἔξω κραθέντα γενέσθαι ζῷον
lexical_decisions.chosen: once put forth by God and blended outside him, they may become a living being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive γενέσθαι can remain under the force of ἐνδέχεται from the preceding clause. The plural substances become one singular living being through blending; “they became” is also possible if the infinitive is understood more assertorically.

lexical_decisions.chosen: carefully distinguished
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rare form conveys deliberate discrimination or separation. “Carefully selected” or “carefully separated” are viable alternatives.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ πρὸς τὸν τῶν κακῶν ὄλεθρον ἐπιθυμία
lexical_decisions.chosen: the desire for the destruction of evil people
lexical_decisions.rationale: τῶν κακῶν may denote evil people or evil things. The personal sense is favored by the preceding κακούς and the subsequent contrast with ἀγαθούς.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after thoroughly examining them, punishes them
lexical_decisions.rationale: διελέγχω can mean examine, expose, refute, or prove guilty. “Thoroughly examining” fits the preceding statement that the evil one initially does not know each person’s character.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ποιεῖν κράσει[ς] πρὸς ἃ βούλεται πρὸς ἃς βούλεται γενέσθαι προαι[ρέ]σεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: to make mixtures for whatever ends he wishes, so that whatever purposes he wishes may arise
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated relatives and shift from neuter ἃ to feminine ἃς leave the attachment compressed. The rendering relates the first phrase to intended ends and the second to προαιρέσεις; alternatively, feminine ἃς may refer directly back to κράσεις.

lexical_decisions.chosen: disposed to choose good things
lexical_decisions.rationale: προαιρετικός with the genitive describes an inclination or capacity to choose the specified objects.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a period after the article. It has no intelligible function as a sentence boundary here and is treated provisionally as an anomalous typographic or editorial punctuation feature, not as unverified text.

passages.text: Peter said, “Our present task is to show how the evil one came to be—if indeed he has come to be—and by whom. As for whether this happened without blame, when I have completed the argument now before us, I will then show how and why he came to be, and I will establish that the one who made him is blameless. Nevertheless, we said that the four substances were put forth by God, and thus, by the intention of the one who combined them, the purpose directed against evil people arose just as he wished. For if it had arisen contrary to his purpose, or from some other substance or even some other cause, God’s plan would not have been secure, since rulers of evil might continually arise against his will and wage war against his designs. But it is impossible for matters to be this way. For no living being—and especially one fit to rule—can come into being by accident, since everything that comes into being must come into being through someone.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: As for whether this happened without blame
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression is elliptical, with the preceding coming-to-be understood. “Whether he came to be blamelessly” is formally possible, but the continuation shows that the issue is whether blame attaches to the maker.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the purpose directed against evil people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive could formally yield “the choice of evil things.” The preceding description explicitly gives the being a purpose to destroy κακούς, favoring an objective genitive directed against evil people.

lexical_decisions.chosen: God’s plan would not have been secure
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, the phrase is “the firmness of the plan.” The rendering expresses the plan’s settled reliability; God is supplied as the contextual possessor.

lexical_decisions.chosen: or even some other cause
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις can denote a cause, occasion, alleged reason, or pretext. “Cause” fits the argument about an independent basis for the evil one’s emergence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: rulers of evil might continually arise
lexical_decisions.rationale: κακίας may identify what these rulers govern or embody. “Leaders in wickedness” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδὲν γὰρ ζῷον καὶ ταῦτα ἡ[γε]μονικὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: no living being—and especially one fit to rule—
lexical_decisions.rationale: καὶ ταῦτα emphasizes an additional noteworthy circumstance: the being is not merely alive but ruling or fitted to command.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by accident
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase denotes coming about incidentally or as a mere chance occurrence, in contrast with production by an agent.

passages.text:
Simon said, “What then? Does matter, being coeternal and equal in power with him, put forth rulers against him as an enemy, rulers who hinder his designs?”

Peter said, “If matter is eternal, it is not anyone’s enemy. For what exists forever is also incapable of suffering; and being incapable of suffering, it is blessed; and being blessed, it cannot become receptive to enmity, since, by its eternal constitution, it has no fear of being deprived of anything. Why, rather, does matter not love the Creator, since it is seen bringing forth fruits as food for all those generated by him? And why has it not feared him as the stronger, as it acknowledges by trembling through earthquakes and as, while surging in great waves, it very quickly obeyed the Teacher, who was sailing and commanded calm, and became quiet? What then? Did the demons not come out while both fearing and honoring him? And did not others first plead to enter pigs, since they did not have authority even to enter pigs without his consent?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ ὕλη αὐτῷ σύγχρονος οὖσα καὶ ἰσοδύναμος
lexical_decisions.chosen: matter, being coeternal and equal in power with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύγχρονος here describes simultaneous eternal existence with God, while ἰσοδύναμος asserts equality of power.

lexical_decisions.chosen: incapable of suffering
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπαθής can mean unaffected, impassible, or incapable of suffering. The argument connects it with freedom from deprivation and fear, so the fuller reader-facing expression is used.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀιδίῳ κτίσει στερηθῆναί τινος μὴ πεφοβημένη
lexical_decisions.chosen: since, by its eternal constitution, it has no fear of being deprived of anything
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative ἀιδίῳ κτίσει has uncertain force. The main rendering understands it causally or instrumentally as matter’s eternal constitution; “in eternal creation” or “as an eternal created thing” are formally conceivable but contextually difficult.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πῶς δ’ οὐχ ὡς κρείττονα πεφόβηται, ὡς καὶ διὰ τῶν σεισμῶν τρέμουσα ὁμολογεῖ καὶ ὡς μεγάλα κυματουμένη τῷ διδασκάλῳ πλέοντι καὶ γαλήνην ἐπιτάξαντι τάχιστα πεισθεῖσα ἡσύχασε;
lexical_decisions.chosen: And why has it not feared him as the stronger, as it acknowledges by trembling through earthquakes and as, while surging in great waves, it very quickly obeyed the Teacher, who was sailing and commanded calm, and became quiet?
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both evidentiary clauses remain attached to the rhetorical question about matter’s fear of the stronger. The dative participles πλέοντι and ἐπιτάξαντι describe the Teacher whom matter obeyed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while both fearing and honoring him
lexical_decisions.rationale: προτιμάω can mean prefer, esteem highly, or honor. The Teacher is the implied object of both infinitives.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς μηδὲ τοῦ εἰς χοίρους εἰσελθεῖν’ ἄνευ τῆς αὐτοῦ συγχωρήσεως ἐξουσίαν ἔχοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: since they did not have authority even to enter pigs without his consent
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς introduces the basis implied by their request, and συγχώρησις here denotes permission or consent.

passages.text:
Simon said, “What then? Although matter is inanimate, does it have a nature capable of producing evil things and good things?”

Peter said, “According to this argument, it is neither good nor evil, because it does not act by choice, being inanimate and insensible. Consequently, here too one can discern how, although it is inanimate, it puts forth animate beings, and how, although it is insensible, it appears to create skillfully formed shapes, both those of animals and those of plants.”

Simon said, “What then? If God himself gave it life, is he not himself the cause, being—this matter gives birth—of evils?”

Peter said, “If God gave it life according to his will, his spirit works upon it, and there is no longer anything hostile to God, equal in power to him, or impossible for him, because everything that comes into being through him comes into being as he wishes. But you will say, ‘He himself is the cause of evil, if indeed he himself produces evil things through it.’ What things, then, will you call evil? Venomous reptiles and deadly plants, or demons, or any other things capable of troubling human beings? These very things—the ..... subtle things—would not have existed if the human being had not sinned, on whose account death entered...... For while the human being existed, reptile venom was not active, the effects of harmful plants did not operate, harassment by demons did not occur, nor did any other suffering naturally belong to him. But when, because of sin, he fell from being immortal, he became, as I said, susceptible to every kind of suffering.

“But if you say, ‘Why, then, was human nature made susceptible to death at the beginning?’ I tell you: because of free choice. For if we had not been susceptible to death, we could not have been punished for freely chosen sin, since we would have been immortal. And thus, because of our incapacity for suffering, even if we were evil in purpose, justice too would have been weakened to some further degree, since those possessing evil purposes would have been unable to be punished because of their incapacity for suffering.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φύσιν ἔχει ἐμφύειν τὰ κακὰ καὶ τὰ ἀγαθά
lexical_decisions.chosen: does it have a nature capable of producing evil things and good things
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐμφύειν can describe causing things to grow, engendering them, or producing them from within.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it is neither good nor evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: Matter is treated as morally neutral because it lacks conscious choice, not because its products are denied all harmful effects.

lexical_decisions.chosen: skillfully formed shapes
lexical_decisions.rationale: τεχνικός here describes forms displaying craft or art rather than the modern sense “technical.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: his spirit works upon it
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐργάζομαι with the accusative presents God’s spirit as acting upon or working matter. “Operates it” is more formally direct, while “works through it” would anticipate the following δι’ αὐτῆς.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐχθρόν τι ἐστιν ἢ ἰσοδύναμον ἢ ἀδύνατον
lexical_decisions.chosen: anything hostile to God, equal in power to him, or impossible for him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative τῷ θεῷ can govern all three adjectives. Thus ἀδύνατον is rendered directly as “impossible for him”; context may imply something beyond God’s power or control, but that implication is not inserted into the text.

lexical_decisions.chosen: venomous reptiles and deadly plants
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἰοβόλος means poison- or venom-casting, while θανάσιμος denotes what is deadly or death-dealing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: These very things—the ..... subtle things—
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἅπερ is emphatic, while λεπτά may mean fine, slight, delicate, or subtle. The exact five-dot printed gap prevents a secure account of the complete phrase, so “subtle” is provisional and the gap remains visible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on whose account death entered
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine relative οὗ most naturally refers to the human being. παρεισέρχομαι depicts death as entering alongside or intruding; “slipped in” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he became susceptible to every kind of suffering
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάθος here includes harmful experiences, afflictions, or suffering, while δεκτικός denotes liability or susceptibility.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of free choice
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτεξούσιον denotes self-determination or freedom within one’s own authority. “Free will” is possible, but “free choice” maintains the connection with προαίρεσις.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for freely chosen sin
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective characterizes the transgression as voluntary or self-determined.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τὸ ἀπαθὲς πλεῖόν τι, κἂν τῇ προαιρέσει ἦμεν κακοί, ἡ καὶ δικαιοσύνη ἐξησθένει
lexical_decisions.chosen: because of our incapacity for suffering, even if we were evil in purpose, justice too would have been weakened to some further degree
lexical_decisions.rationale: πλεῖόν τι is loosely positioned and may mean “somewhat more” or “in some greater respect.” The rendering takes it with ἐξησθένει and preserves its comparative force without supplying an unstated standard.

source_issues.source_quote: οὐκ αὐτὸς αἴτιός ἐστιν ὢν αὕτη τίκτει κακῶν;
source_issues.issue: The selected edition’s verified reading ὢν is a masculine nominative participle, but no defensible continuous syntax has been established for its relationship to αἴτιός ἐστιν, the intervening finite clause αὕτη τίκτει, and κακῶν. The translation mechanically preserves the sequence through the deliberately unresolved wording “the cause, being—this matter gives birth—of evils” rather than silently supplying a conjunction or relative construction. The conjecture ὧν would yield the coherent sense “is he not himself the cause of the evils that this matter begets?”, but that is not the supplied reading and has not been adopted.
source_issues.proposed_reading: οὐκ αὐτὸς αἴτιός ἐστιν ὧν αὕτη τίκτει κακῶν;

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a lacuna of exactly five dots between τὰ and λεπτὰ. Its content is unavailable, and no restoration has been supplied; the five-dot gap is retained explicitly in the translation.

The selected edition prints a lacuna of exactly six dots before γὰρ. Its content is unavailable and has not been restored. The six-dot gap is retained at the corresponding boundary after “entered,” and the surviving genitive absolute is translated separately as “For while the human being existed.”
